name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,151

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A clown, Mario’s one who dies in a tale of crime

definitions.text: Mario’s one who dies in a tale of crime

blocks.note: first meaning: a jester or buffoon

blocks.clueFragment: Mario’s one who dies in a tale of crime
blocks.note: second meaning: Mario Puzo's later crime novel has a title saying such silly people perish

explanation.surface: A clown is killed off in an Italian crime story.
explanation.walkthrough: Mario is Mario Puzo, author of The Godfather; his later novel is titled Fools Die, so its singular victim gives the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A jester at court was called by this name, and Puzo's title uses the same noun for silly people who perish.

clue.text: Expose hoax? It’s what one writer may want to do to another

definitions.text: what one writer may want to do to another

blocks.note: to out someone is to expose them
a sell is an old word for a trick or hoax

explanation.surface: Unmasking a fraud is what one author might relish doing to a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes the first two words look like a literary scandal; they are simply two pieces placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Rival authors compete on sales, so beating another's book figures is a natural professional ambition.

clue.text: Male lover not ridiculous for a poet with Scottish roots

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and disordered, so the letters before it are put into a silly new order

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man's lover insists he is not ridiculous, on behalf of a poet of Scottish descent.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first letter of 'Male' joins the fodder. Mikhail Lermontov, the Russian Romantic poet, descended from a Scottish soldier named Learmonth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian Romantic writer traced his family to a seventeenth-century Scottish mercenary, giving him ancestry north of the border.

clue.text: Reject lad with trifling gains – one falsely accused of theft

blocks.note: small gains are wins that are low
a lad is a boy; 'Reject' fits the story, where the boy is expelled from naval college

explanation.surface: An outcast youth makes paltry profits and is wrongly charged with stealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue in reverse order, joined by 'with'. In Terence Rattigan's play, young Ronnie Winslow is expelled from naval college over a stolen postal order.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattigan's title character is a cadet wrongly blamed for stealing five shillings, and his family fights to clear his name.

clue.text: Tumbledown winter home is for one exiled in the Borders

indicators.note: a tumbledown building has collapsed into disorder, so the following letters fall into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written: fifteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A ramshackle winter house belongs to someone banished to the Scottish Borders.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stevenson's unfinished novel, the hanging judge's son Archie Weir is banished to the family estate of Hermiston; the Borders is the region of Scotland next to England.
explanation.definitionFit: Archie, heir to the Hermiston estate, is sent away to that remote Borders property by his stern father, so he is the exile.

clue.text: One with no support – no great shakes

indicators.note: to shake something is to jumble it, so the preceding words are tossed into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone without backing is dismissed as nothing special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No great shakes' is an idiom for mediocre, which hides the split between the fodder and the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who denies or contradicts gives no support to a proposal, so this person is a naysayer.

clue.text: Spankers appear in this city with complete confidence

definitions.note: a description of the play rather than a synonym

blocks.note: the city, the British capital
assurance is full self-confidence

explanation.surface: People who administer beatings swagger about town with total self-belief.
explanation.walkthrough: Spankers are not punishers but characters: Lady Gay Spanker and her husband Dolly appear in Dion Boucicault's 1841 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Boucicault's comedy of manners features the hunting-mad Lady Gay Spanker, so the Spanker couple are among its cast.

clue.text: “Oh, give me again the rover’s life – the joy, the thrill, the — ” (Herman Melville, White Jacket)

definitions.text: “Oh, give me again the rover’s life – the joy, the thrill, the — ” (Herman Melville, White Jacket)

blocks.clueFragment: “Oh, give me again the rover’s life – the joy, the thrill, the — ”
blocks.note: surface reading: a sailor longing for life at sea, with the last word of the list missing
setter's reading: the source names Melville's novel of navy life, which supplies the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the gap is filled from Melville's White-Jacket, where the narrator yearns for the excitement of a seafaring life.
explanation.definitionFit: A rush of giddy activity rounds off the list of excitements, matching joy and thrill as nouns of exhilaration.

clue.text: Curious couplet describing the Snark’s fits

definitions.note: an adjective defined by what it describes

indicators.note: something curious is odd or strange, so the following letters take an unusual new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd pair of rhyming lines describes the seizures of Lewis Carroll's creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fits' are not seizures but cantos: Carroll subtitled The Hunting of the Snark 'An Agony in Eight Fits'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's nonsense poem is divided into eight sections called fits, so the set of them is eightfold.

clue.text: What can link actor to film? Looking fashionable – that’s about right

definitions.text: What can link actor to film?

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one word wraps itself round another

blocks.note: staring is looking hard
R is the abbreviation for right
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A question about casting, answered by someone who looks smart and is told that's correct.
explanation.walkthrough: The R goes inside the first word, then the second follows. 'About' sits after 'that's', so it reads as approximation rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Credits say an actor is billed in a lead role in a movie, so these two words connect performer to picture.

clue.text: Something trivial in the Riot Act

indicators.note: 'in' says the wanted letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A petty offence earns someone a formal reprimand.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading the Riot Act is an idiom for a severe telling-off; the answer straddles its last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest Greek letter has become an idiom for a tiny amount, a trifle or jot.

clue.text: This month featuring in ode rewritten anew

indicators.note: to feature in something is to appear within it, so one piece sits inside the other
a text rewritten is recast, so these letters are set down in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
NOV is the calendar abbreviation for November, when the puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: A poem revised to mention the current month is made fresh again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This month' depends on the publication date: the puzzle ran in November 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means starting over from the beginning, used in English for doing something afresh.

clue.text: Earlier author’s flow of words, comprehended by Beat poet

indicators.note: to beat is to batter or whisk, so the following word is knocked into a new order
to comprehend is literally to grasp or include, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written
a roll is a rolling, rhythmic flow of speech

explanation.surface: An older writer's eloquence is understood by a Beat Generation poet like Ginsberg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat poet' looks like Kerouac or Ginsberg, but 'Beat' is the instruction applied to 'poet'. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope wrote Victorian novels, so he predates the Beats by a century and counts as an older writer.

clue.text: This playwright lived with an artist

blocks.note: fl. (floruit, 'flourished') marks when someone lived and worked
an etcher is an artist who makes prints from etched plates

explanation.surface: A dramatist shared a home with a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to John Fletcher, who famously shared lodgings with his collaborator Beaumont. FL is the reference-book abbreviation for floruit, Latin for 'he flourished'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fletcher was a Jacobean dramatist who collaborated with Beaumont and Shakespeare.

clue.text: Thriller writer’s left in an indication of danger

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: an amber light warns of danger ahead
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A suspense novelist has been abandoned in a perilous situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb, abandoned, but it supplies a single letter. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Ambler wrote spy and suspense novels such as The Mask of Dimitrios, classics of the genre.

clue.text: Southern story, lots of it filmed

blocks.note: first meaning: the title of a 1970 novel by Terry Southern
second meaning: 'it' is sex appeal, so a film with plenty of sex in it

explanation.surface: A tale from the American South, much of it shot on camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern' is not the region but the satirist Terry Southern, co-writer of Dr Strangelove. 'It' is the old slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A pornographic film contains plenty of sex, and Southern used that phrase as his satirical novel's title.

clue.text: Orwell’s horse blanket concealing a bit of Lippizaner

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece wraps the other
just a bit of the word is taken, its opening letter

blocks.note: a blanket is a cover
the first letter of the horse breed

explanation.surface: A horse rug hides part of an elegant Viennese white horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Lipizzaners are the white horses of Vienna's Spanish Riding School, a natural fit for a horse blanket.
explanation.definitionFit: In Animal Farm, the motherly mare who cares for the other animals carries this name.

clue.text: Greek city featured in Doctor Zhivago

blocks.note: first meaning: the capital of Thessaly
second meaning: the full first name of Lara, the heroine of Pasternak's novel

explanation.surface: A Greek town appears in Pasternak's epic.
explanation.walkthrough: The heroine everyone knows as Lara is Larissa Fyodorovna in full; Lara is the short form.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thessalian city and Pasternak's heroine share the same name, a Greek-derived given name.

clue.text: In Spain, a house suitable for everyone – in France, good for a priest from the English Midlands

definitions.text: a priest from the English Midlands

blocks.note: casa is Spanish for house
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing
bon is French for good

explanation.surface: A Spanish house fit for all and a French blessing on a cleric from central England.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British cinema rating meaning anyone may watch. The 'English Midlands' points to George Eliot's Middlemarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reverend Edward Casaubon, Dorothea's dry scholar husband, is the clergyman of Middlemarch, a fictional Midlands town.

clue.text: Dramatically a nephew (unknown) replacing son in Dickens

indicators.note: replacing means one thing takes another's place, so one letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: the novelist's first name
S is the abbreviation for son
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns

explanation.surface: In Dickens, an unidentified nephew takes over from a son.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the final S off the novelist's first name and put a Y in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: In Brandon Thomas's farce Charley's Aunt, the title character is the nephew of the rich widow Donna Lucia.

clue.text: Spells of cricket and running partly coincide

blocks.note: an over is a spell of six balls bowled in cricket
a lap is a spell of running round a track

explanation.surface: Periods of cricket and running are partly simultaneous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spells' does double duty, applying to both sports: an over is a set of six deliveries from one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that share some area or time without matching completely extend over each other in part.

clue.text: One seen flirting with Greek in play is scared

indicators.note: something in play is moving about freely, so the letters are loose to rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone flirting with a Greek in a drama is frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In play' seems to belong to the definition, a character in a play, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, the Trojan heroine is handed to the Greek camp and dallies with Diomedes.

clue.text: Very successful author’s bargain book announced?

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so what matters is how the word sounds

blocks.note: a bargain is a steal, here a book sold cheaply

explanation.surface: A bestselling writer's novel being sold off cheap.
explanation.walkthrough: Danielle Steel has sold hundreds of millions of romance novels. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Danielle Steel is among the best-selling novelists of all time, so she is a hugely popular writer.

clue.text: Mummy, damned in a vampire expert’s work

definitions.text: Mummy, damned in a vampire expert’s work

blocks.note: surface reading: a cursed mummy, a horror trope
setter's reading: Anne Rice, author of the vampire chronicles, wrote The Mummy, whose title character is the pharaoh called the Damned

explanation.surface: A cursed mummy turns up in the work of a vampire specialist.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'vampire expert' is not Van Helsing but Anne Rice, whose 1989 novel is The Mummy, or Ramses the Damned.
explanation.definitionFit: Rice's title names the immortal Egyptian pharaoh as the cursed mummy of her story.

clue.text: Junk lies somewhere off the coast

indicators.note: to junk something is to scrap it, so the following word is broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Chinese sailing boat is moored just offshore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junk' reads as the Chinese ship, but it is the instruction acting on 'lies'.
explanation.definitionFit: An island is a piece of land surrounded by sea, often lying a short way from the mainland.

clue.text: Striking a level tone in Latin America drama

indicators.note: striking means hitting, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Speaking in a flat, even voice in a Latin American play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' reads as 'impressive' or 'adopting', but it is the instruction for the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin American television soap opera, usually melodramatic and running for a limited season, goes by this name.

clue.text: a major figure in children’s literature

definitions.text: a major figure in children’s literature

blocks.note: surface reading: an important name in general
setter's reading: a Victorian Scottish author of adventure stories for boys

explanation.walkthrough: R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Coral Island and many other adventure stories that shaped Victorian children's reading.
explanation.definitionFit: His desert-island tale inspired Golding's Lord of the Flies, a sign of his lasting influence on young readers' books.

clue.text: David Hare’s clergyman with sixth sense? Unknown

blocks.note: ESP, extrasensory perception, is called the sixth sense
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns

explanation.surface: A playwright's vicar seems to have psychic powers of unknown origin.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer looks like the verb 'to catch sight of', but here it is a surname: the Reverend Lionel Espy of Hare's play Racing Demon.
explanation.definitionFit: Hare's 1990 drama about the Church of England centres on a doubting south London vicar with this surname.
